body:
This seems reasonable to me as a concept, lthough I am not convinced that it's enough value added to justify the effort in all implementations on a legacy API. (As opposed to just returning false.) Do we think that pages that use confirm are really maintained by developers, as opposed to being relics from the past?

I guess I'd prefer if we had either strong signals from web developers that they'd use this (although, if they're updating that code anyway, can they move away from this horrible API?), or signs that more implementers are OK spending time on this, or both. Or some reason this would help Chrome to deprecate/make better the confirm API, which would not be achievable by returning false.

I don't think there's any reason other implementations would necessarily need to do any work here - they'd automatically conform to the spec without ever returning `null`.  But if eg. Safari wanted to move away from it's hang-prone message-loop-blocking model, then this tweak would potentially give them a little more flexibility in doing so.

I'd be OK with trying to just use `false` in all such cases and wait to hear if a single developer complains (then probably reverting to buy us some time), but often by then some damage has been done (especially if we don't get their complaint until the impacted Chrome release hits stable - as is likely in the case of Enterprise customers).

I think there are three aspects of the [blink compat principles](https://docs.google.com/document/d/1RC-pBBvsazYfCNNUSkPqAVpSpNJ96U8trhNkfV0v9fk) which speak to this:

- [Debuggability](https://docs.google.com/document/d/1RC-pBBvsazYfCNNUSkPqAVpSpNJ96U8trhNkfV0v9fk/edit#heading=h.axcg738lzcs9): it's more likely that a developer will be able to quickly figure out what's going on by noticing the new return value.
 - [Ease of adaptation](https://docs.google.com/document/d/1RC-pBBvsazYfCNNUSkPqAVpSpNJ96U8trhNkfV0v9fk/edit#heading=h.x5bhg5grhfeo): There are some scenarios (like my banking scenario) where being able to treat the two cases differently is much easier to do than to completely change their code.  Eg. for browsers that continue to support tab activation they would likely prefer to keep using `confirm`, and for those that don't they may prefer to fall back to `alert` if it will give the user some indication the tab needs attention.  We also know that developers are much grumpier about breakage that requires non-trivial changes (like introducing entire new UI elements) than those that require trivial changes (we've see large numbers of sites update en-masse without a single complaint raised to chromium when the changes are trivial and easy to learn about).  IMHO if we cause even one more developer to file a bug or post to blink-dev than they would otherwise we've already made the wrong choice (because for each such developer there are likely 100 that are suffering in silence hating the web a little bit more).
 - [Severity of breakage](https://docs.google.com/document/d/1RC-pBBvsazYfCNNUSkPqAVpSpNJ96U8trhNkfV0v9fk/edit#heading=h.u5ya6jvru7dl): It's possible that introducing the new value could break things worse than re-using `false`.

I'm not sure what the right balance between these are.  If folks here feel like overloading `false` for these cases is better, then I'd be fine starting with that and seeing if we get developer complaints.  But my personal instinct is that we mitigate the harm more at very little cause by introducing the `null` option.  But again, I wouldn't suggest actually landing a spec change for this until we've proven it's web compatible.

I don't see how other browsers would be compliant without changing their code. Don't several of them auto-dismiss in the background already? (I've lost track unfortunately.) I know Firefox also has a checkbox to suppress the popups (just tested). All those cases are cases where the user didn't interact, so the spec would require returning null.

If the idea is to just add an optional ability to return null, that's not great; we try very hard to not add optional features to the spec. None of the benefits you list in compat principles are available to developers if they can't rely on this new return value across browsers and scenarios, so we'd want to move the ecosystem as a whole, not just add an optional feature for Chrome only.

> I don't see how other browsers would be compliant without changing their code. Don't several of them auto-dismiss in the background already?

No, as far as I know Chrome is the only one to auto-dismiss at this point.  They suppress background activation but they do so without auto-dismissing see [Avi's doc](https://docs.google.com/document/d/1wtV5rmLhbf1OZkbg7crtCt6h1mMtig_ctTQt3BLLEIU/edit) and a trivial test page [here](http://output.jsbin.com/tuwuno).

>  I know Firefox also has a checkbox to suppress the popups (just tested). All those cases are cases where the user didn't interact, so the spec would require returning null.

Ah, that's a good point - I verified that Firefox does indeed return `false` in such cases (multiple dialogs, user selects option to prevent future ones).

> If the idea is to just add an optional ability to return null, that's not great

Agreed.  So I think our option is to proceed with using `false` or see if Firefox is interested in joining us in returning `null`.  I only now realized that the spec already [defines](https://html.spec.whatwg.org/#dom-confirm) `false` as the return value to be used when the dialog isn't shown.  So there's already a compelling argument to developers of that banking scenario I mentioned that their dialog should correctly be worded in the inverse way: "Ok to remain logged in, Cancel to logout".

Given that and the precedent from Firefox I'm now leaning towards saying we should continue to overload `false` in the absence of concrete developer requests to differentiate.  @avidrissman WDYT?
Let's close this then, although I'm happy to reopen if the situation changes and we think this is still an important path to try.
